en: Hearing this, Chyntengir said:
“The Ala-Too is no land for us;
The old enemy, the vile Burut,
Will never be a people to us.
Inflict harsh torment;
Silence his tongue without delay.
Bring his death upon him now,
Deprive him of every recourse.
Cut strips of hide from his back;
You blood-drinking champions,
Seize him and take his life!
Cut off his sheep-like head;
Rip open his melon-like belly!”
Thus Chyntengir spoke,
Urging and dispatching
His champions and giants,
Rousing and dispatching
His strongest heroes.
His champions and warriors
Now began to trample and beat him,
Inflicting every torture they knew.
They tormented and took his life,
Cutting off his hands and feet.
The champions attacked
The noble gray-maned hero
And took his precious head;
They finished him then and there.
“We slaughtered and destroyed the champion
Whose stars crossed ours.”
Breaking through the dead end and opening a road,
The Chinese army attacked directly
Against the true Black Kyrgyz.
Alymsaryk and hero Kulan,
Defenders of all the people,
Fought a vicious fight,
Standing face-to-face,
Fighting turn by turn,
Locked in a bloody struggle.
Their father, gray-maned Jeljetpes,
Was protecting the twin heroes,
So the champion's line might endure.
He turned summer's day into winter,
And plunged the Chinese and Kakan troops
Who came against them into calamity.
He sent a flood and made it water.
The three heroes raised an uproar,
Cutting through the standing Chinese host.
Supporting one another,
They were drenched in bloody dust,
And fought without turning back.
Jeljetpes moved through their midst;
Wounded in seven places,
He had a net spread before him.
After countless heroes
From the Beijing host thrust at him,
His life was truly scorched.
He was snatched from certain death,
Caught in the fatal net,
Yet Jeljetpes broke free and escaped.
Alymsaryk and Kulansaryk,
Two fair heroes with rhyming names,
Passed through the solitary foe.
Their muscular flesh was torn,
And the flesh of their ribs ripped away;
The two reached a quiet place.
Climbing to a mountain pass, they leaned down,
And on a truly sacred hill
They dozed and fell asleep.
Their closed eyes would not open,
Their outstretched legs would not draw in,
And their deep snoring did not cease.
They sank into a giant's sleep.
Jeljetpes and the twin heroes
Let the horses they had ridden to war
Cool fully and drink their fill.
They grazed them on feather grass,
Led them a little while,
And filled their throats with grass;
Led them a long while,
And filled their chests with grass.
This is the spirit of your dear father,
[Meaning uncertain: opening word unresolved.]
His first ancestor was a khan,
He used to support him from the beginning [reading uncertain],
Kara Kozhal was of the Arabs,
Of the hero Booruk Kenen,
He was the one appointed,
Father Kalka became khan,
[Meaning uncertain: opening words unresolved.]
Making a people by Heaven's will,
Making the strength of his weapons,
Making the gathered clans a people,
Though oppressed, he grew mighty,
Multiplying from solitude,
Becoming the equal of the whole world,
Arstan Kozhal, the brave warrior,
Finding no mountain to dash against [reading uncertain],
Finding no enemy to wage war against,
Those people who heeded words,
He made into a people with his speech,
The fool who would not heed words,
He bent by force to his will,
No one had dared face him,
Saying, “Valiant Kenen, conquer!”,
He spared no enemy side,
The horse he rode was a bay charger,
Where the bay charger had not trotted or walked,
No land remained intact,
That Kenen did not demand and take,
No people remained intact,
That had not tried a cunning stratagem,
None of the cunning remained intact,
That Kyrgyz Kenen had not struck,
None among the peoples remained intact,
[Meaning uncertain: pale line unresolved.]
The foremost warrior born into the world,
Eloquent in speech, a wise man,
He granted whatever was wished,
He beat back the wrathful,
He reconciled what could not be reconciled,
Whatever anyone said to me,
He supplied an answer to them all,
Dust rose as though the earth had stirred,
A murmuring host came forth,
No man dared approach him face to face,
Narrow in temper, he would not open his hand,
The radiance never left his face.
Keeping companions, he gathered brave men,
From Tölögön's people he gathered his peers,
The land sustained their great chiefs,
Gathering the multitude, he cared for the people,
His thousand warriors who laid siege,
All those who had wandered,
Filling sacks with yellow gold,
Thinking deeply, he sustained the people,
Taking on the fury of a tiger,
He came to be called Kenen the Tiger,
Making the hero's arrow ready,
The enemy who poured out his wrath,
He destroyed him and drew blood,
No people remained to speak against him,
Saying, 'The mighty Kozhal has fallen,'
From his father to his forefathers,
Like a treasure upon his head,
Saying that fortune and prosperity had settled upon him,
The people spoke throughout the great realm,
Saying he had become the father of the people,
Whenever he seemed spent, he flared up anew,
He had grown strong from his very roots.
After each one died, in pursuit,
I myself led those who would strike them down,
[Uncertain: will they find the cart-load, frozen?]
His heroism is great as well.
His own eyes saw it clearly,
The foremost sage,
Racing across the face of the earth,
He would emerge alone from the race,
His four racehorses were ready,
From Saykal, whom the prince had taken,
There was a soul who followed behind me.
Settling them on two summer pastures,
Was it the multitude that migrated?
I lived in freedom,
Delighting the people, he went laughing,
He had become the people's enclosure and refuge,
His heroism, his lionhearted courage,
Now it struck the palate like springtime,
If he roared fearsomely,
His eyes reddening like a lion's,
[Uncertain: his mouth like a bow ...]
Stretching out across the open steppe,
With a hundred close companions,
His comrades were brave men,
[Uncertain: seething, equal in merriment,]
When a black gun cracked,
Brave Kenen, who would not flee,
When a great gun boomed,
Lionhearted Kenen would not startle and flee,
His majesty mounting, his wrath sharp,
Noble Kenen, the gray-maned wolf,
[Uncertain: come as a somewhat superior equal,]
